title: Breaking Down Organizational Silos
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece diagnoses organizational silos as one of the most common and corrosive dysfunctions leaders face, rooted in divisions that have no felt reason to communicate because their day-to-day success doesn't visibly depend on it. Rather than treating silos as an intractable cultural problem, the author lays out two concrete, reliable strategies for dismantling them: assigning joint accountability for shared results, and building genuinely significant cross-functional initiatives staffed by credible opinion leaders. The piece argues that once leaders are made jointly responsible for outcomes, the incentive to withhold information or protect turf collapses naturally. It closes by pushing back on the common objection that joint accountability "makes no sense" in a siloed structure, framing that resistance as a lack of imagination rather than a real barrier.
points: Silos persist because leaders in siloed divisions genuinely don't see how information from other areas affects their own success — and they're often technically right.
Shared, joint accountability for results is the single most pivotal lever for dissolving silos, because it removes the incentive to withhold information.
Cross-functional initiatives only erode silos when the projects are genuinely significant and staffed by leaders who already carry credibility within their own segment.
When siloed leaders object that joint accountability "makes no sense," that resistance is a failure of imagination, not evidence the approach won't work.
quotes: Of the many dysfunctions suffered by organizations, perhaps none is more common or corrosive than silos.
In a highly siloed organization, leaders don't talk to one another. They simply don't believe they have any reason to.

Breaking down silos depends on defining shared accountability. When leaders are jointly responsible for outcomes and own results together, they quickly learn to drop the pretenses and begin to collaborate.
In order for this strategy to have a lasting impact, the projects must be significant and the leaders involved should be highly credible within their segment of the organization.
When siloed leaders suggest that creating joint accountability makes no sense, don't believe them. They simply need a push and a spark of creative insight to see things anew.
